paragraphs: Lane detection becomes difficult when vehicles hide road markings or poor lighting makes them hard to distinguish. Methods that locate lane key points mainly from fine image details can struggle because those details may be unreliable. This paper proposes a Siamese Transformer that combines broader scene information with local features to improve detection in complex road environments.

Its central component, LAne TRansformer, refines lane key points through a high-to-low hierarchy. Global semantic information contributes context, while finer features help determine precise positions. The method also introduces Curve-IoU, a training loss designed around the thin, elongated shape of lane lines. This gives the model supervision directed at how well the predicted curves fit the lanes.

Experiments on three lane detection benchmarks report state-of-the-art results with high accuracy and efficiency. On OpenLane, the reported F1 score exceeds the previous best-performing method by 5.0 points. These findings support combining contextual refinement with a shape-aware training objective for the evaluated lane detection tasks.
neurips-2024-a-siamese-transformer-with-.tldr: A hierarchical Siamese Transformer combines scene context, local features, and a lane-shaped loss to improve lane detection.

paragraphs: Neural activity sequences can provide a timing framework for behavior, but maintaining them is challenging when connections continually change. Inspired by a songbird circuit that supports song timing and recovers after disruption, this paper searches for local learning rules that can both create and maintain sequence-generating activity.

The researchers use meta-learning to tune rules built from activity on either side of a synapse, synapse strength, and adjustable time constants. They simulate candidate rules in initially random networks and evaluate how faithfully the resulting activity represents time. Introducing biological noise during this search encourages rules that remain useful under perturbation.

Without perturbations, the search finds a temporally asymmetric extension of Oja's rule that organizes sparse sequences. With synaptic turnover, learned rules add homeostatic behavior and maintain sequences better than previously proposed alternatives. Allowing plasticity at inhibitory as well as excitatory connections further improves responses to manipulation. The findings show how jointly adapting excitation and inhibition can support more resilient timing representations in these simulated circuits.
neurips-2024-discovering-plasticity-rule.tldr: Meta-learning discovers local plasticity rules that organize neural sequences and better preserve them under network perturbations.

paragraphs: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal how molecular systems move, but their computational cost motivates learned substitutes. This paper treats molecular trajectories as objects that a generative model can learn to produce. The aim is a flexible surrogate that supports several tasks through different choices of conditioning information.

Conditioning on selected trajectory frames lets the model perform forward simulation, sample paths between states, or fill in additional frames to make a trajectory more temporally detailed. A second form of conditioning specifies part of the molecular system and generates the remainder. The authors present this as an initial step toward designing molecules with information about their dynamics.

The full collection of capabilities is validated on tetrapeptide simulations, with preliminary results for protein monomers. The contribution is therefore both a shared modeling approach and a demonstration of its versatility at the tested scale. It shows how existing simulation data can support downstream questions beyond straightforward forward prediction, while the protein results remain an early indication of scalability.
neurips-2024-generative-modeling-of-mole.tldr: Generative trajectory models use different conditioning choices to support molecular simulation, path sampling, temporal upsampling, and early dynamics-guided design.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how strongly several labels apply to an example, rather than assigning only one label or a set of labels. This paper brings that problem to heterogeneous graphs, where nodes can differ in type, attributes, and surrounding connections. Those differences complicate how information should be combined to predict a node's label distribution.

The proposed framework first learns how to aggregate information across meta-paths, which describe different patterns of connections through the graph. This topology homogenization addresses heterogeneity before node representations are learned. A graph transformer then uses attention to capture consistency between these structural patterns and node attributes, giving both topology and content a role in prediction.

Training combines KL divergence with additional constraints to learn the system end to end. The authors report theoretical and empirical support for the approach. Its central contribution is a framework that explicitly handles heterogeneous graph structure while preserving the richer prediction target of a distribution over labels.
neurips-2024-hgdl-heterogeneous-graph-la.tldr: HGDL predicts label distributions on heterogeneous graphs by coordinating structural aggregation with attention to node attributes.

paragraphs: Diffusion models work well empirically, but explaining their data requirements remains a theoretical challenge. This paper asks how many training examples are sufficient to learn an accurate diffusion model when the neural network is expressive enough. That question concerns the statistical cost of obtaining the model in the first place.

The analysis focuses on sample complexity, complementing work on how many iterations are needed to generate samples once an accurate model is available. Earlier training bounds depended polynomially on dimension and on accuracy requirements expressed through total variation and Wasserstein error. The new results improve these guarantees, including an exponential improvement in their dependence on Wasserstein error and depth.

The authors also report better dependence on other relevant parameters. These are improvements to mathematical bounds on training data requirements, so their significance lies in a sharper account of what learning can require under the stated expressivity assumption. The result helps distinguish the difficulty of learning a diffusion model from the separate difficulty of sampling with it.
neurips-2024-improved-sample-complexity-.tldr: The paper sharpens diffusion training sample-complexity bounds, exponentially improving their dependence on Wasserstein error and depth.

paragraphs: Augmented Lagrangian methods are widely used to solve constrained optimization problems. For conic programs, previous theory established linear convergence of dual iterates and optimality residuals under a quadratic growth assumption. The remaining question concerned the primal iterates: the actual sequence of candidate solutions to the original optimization problem.

This paper develops new quadratic growth and error bound properties for both primal and dual conic programs under strict complementarity. These properties connect the geometry of the optimization problem with how closely an iterate approaches a solution. They provide the theoretical ingredients needed to analyze primal convergence alongside the already studied dual behavior.

The main result establishes linear convergence of both primal and dual iterates under strict complementarity and a bounded solution set. Linear convergence describes an eventual geometric rate of improvement, making the result more informative than convergence alone. The conclusion resolves the stated open question about asymptotic primal convergence, with the guarantee explicitly tied to those problem assumptions.
neurips-2024-inexact-augmented-lagrangia.tldr: Under strict complementarity and a bounded solution set, augmented Lagrangian methods have linear convergence of both primal and dual iterates.

paragraphs: Predicting the next visual state becomes easier when a sequence follows a relatively straight path in its internal representation. Inspired by observations of primate vision, this paper develops a self-supervised objective that directly measures and encourages this straightening. A straighter trajectory can support prediction by continuing its current direction through linear extrapolation.

The researchers train deep feedforward networks on smoothly rendered synthetic image sequences designed to reproduce common properties of natural videos. The resulting representations are predictive and also separate geometric, photometric, and semantic object attributes. Thus, the training objective affects both how representations evolve over time and how they organize different aspects of an image.

Compared with earlier self-supervised methods based on invariance to random augmentations, the learned representations show greater robustness to noise and adversarial attacks. Adding straightening as a regularizer also transfers beneficial properties to other training procedures. These results support its potential as a broader learning principle, with the main demonstrations grounded in the synthetic sequence setting.
neurips-2024-learning-predictable-and-ro.tldr: Encouraging straight trajectories through representation space produces predictive, factorized, and more robust visual embeddings in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Studies of language model internals often analyze a single checkpoint, even though deployed models may continue training. This paper investigates whether the mechanisms identified at one point remain informative later. It tracks circuits in decoder-only language models over 300 billion training tokens, covering models with 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters.

Across these scales, task abilities and the functional components supporting them emerge at similar token counts. Individual attention heads implementing a component can change over training, while the broader algorithm remains consistent. The researchers also find that these algorithms and component types tend to recur across model sizes.

Circuit size behaves less uniformly: it correlates with model size and can fluctuate substantially even when the implemented algorithm stays the same. This separates stability of computation from stability of the particular components carrying it out. The findings suggest that analyses of small models after pretraining can yield insights relevant after further training and at larger scales, within the scope of the studied models.
neurips-2024-llm-circuit-analyses-are-co.tldr: Studied language-model circuits often retain similar algorithms across training and scale even as their implementing heads and sizes change.

paragraphs: Answering visual questions can require several kinds of information at once: recognizing image content, applying background knowledge, interpreting symbols or diagrams, and following a sequence of reasoning steps. Meteor uses rich rationales to bring these forms of information into a language-and-vision model's training.

The method employs Mamba to process lengthy rationales efficiently, drawing on its linear-time handling of sequential data. A proposed rationale traversal mechanism embeds this information, after which the backbone multimodal language model is trained to generate answers with help from the rationale. This makes the treatment of explanatory information a central part of the training approach.

The authors report significant improvements across multiple vision-language benchmarks covering diverse capabilities. These gains are achieved without increasing model size or adding vision encoders or other computer vision models. The results suggest that improving how a model incorporates multifaceted rationales can strengthen its visual understanding and answering capabilities while retaining the stated architectural scale.
neurips-2024-meteor-mamba-based-traversa.tldr: Meteor uses Mamba to embed rich rationales efficiently, improving vision-language performance without enlarging the model or adding vision encoders.

paragraphs: Movement during an MRI scan can introduce severe artifacts into reconstructed images and volumes. MotionTTT estimates that movement at test time so the reconstruction can account for it. Its key idea is to use a network trained for motion-free reconstruction as a guide for finding motion parameters.

The approach relies on the reconstruction network producing a small loss when motion is absent. It therefore optimizes motion parameters through the network, seeking parameters that make the reconstruction consistent with that behavior. Although the reconstruction networks operate in two dimensions, the method estimates rigid motion in three dimensions and uses those estimates to reconstruct corrected images.

The paper proves motion-parameter recovery for a simplified signal and neural network model. It also evaluates the method using both retrospectively simulated movement and prospectively collected measurements containing real movement. Together, these results provide a theoretical demonstration in a simple setting and empirical support on motion-corrupted data for the proposed route to three-dimensional motion correction.
neurips-2024-motionttt-2d-test-time-trai.tldr: MotionTTT optimizes three-dimensional rigid motion estimates through two-dimensional reconstruction networks to correct motion-corrupted MRI.

paragraphs: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis concerns whether a large random neural network already contains a subnetwork that approximates a given sufficiently smaller network without training. Earlier results established such approximation but did not guarantee how small the selected subnetwork would be. This paper adds guarantees on subnetwork sparsity.

The technical obstacle lies in random subset sum arguments. These ask whether numbers from a random sample can be selected so their sum approximates a desired value. A successful approximation alone does not control how many numbers are selected. The paper studies a fixed-size version of this problem, where the chosen subset must have a specified size, and proves an essentially tight bound.

That bound supports sparsity guarantees for the strong lottery ticket hypothesis in settings including dense and equivariant networks. The contribution connects the existence of accurate untrained subnetworks with control over their size. The fixed-size subset sum result is also presented as independently useful beyond its role in the neural network proofs.
neurips-2024-on-the-sparsity-of-the-stro.tldr: A fixed-size random subset sum bound yields strong lottery ticket results that also guarantee subnetwork sparsity.

paragraphs: Kernel methods depend partly on how well the function being learned aligns with the structure represented by the kernel matrix. This paper analyzes that relationship for a broad family of losses covering regression and classification. It compares a standard kernel method with one restricted to a reduced space obtained by spectral truncation.

The analysis uses a kernel complexity function to bound the behavior of both methods and expose their dependence on alignment. For polynomially decaying alignment, the methods have the same learning rate in the just-aligned and weakly aligned regimes. With strong alignment, however, the standard method reaches a saturation point while the truncated method continues to benefit as alignment strengthens.

This identifies a setting where reducing the function space can capture favorable target structure more effectively. A minimax lower bound for squared loss establishes the truncated method's optimality in that analysis. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings, while the claimed advantage remains tied to the alignment regimes and loss conditions being studied.
neurips-2024-on-the-target-kernel-alignm.tldr: Spectral truncation lets kernel methods keep benefiting from strong target alignment in regimes where standard methods saturate.

paragraphs: In dueling bandits, a learner selects pairs of options and learns from their comparisons. This paper studies weak regret, where presenting one optimal option is enough to avoid loss. It assumes a stochastic setting with a Condorcet winner: an option that wins against each alternative in pairwise comparisons.

Existing strategies can bound weak regret independently of the time horizon, but that leaves open how the bound should depend on the problem itself. The authors show why the winner's smallest advantage over other options matters alongside the wider comparison structure. When this minimum gap is not negligible relative to other properties of the gap matrix, they characterize the optimal regret budget in terms of the number of options and the gap.

A proposed strategy achieves that optimum and improves the corresponding dependence over prior methods. When the gap is negligible, a second algorithm outperforms the first. Numerical simulations assess the theory, highlighting that different comparison structures can favor different exploration strategies even under the same weak-regret objective.
neurips-2024-on-weak-regret-analysis-for.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal weak regret in a dueling-bandit regime and develops strategies suited to different winner-gap structures.

paragraphs: An online learner repeatedly chooses an action while trying to limit cumulative loss. This paper asks how much it helps to occasionally know the best action before choosing. Such advance information is modeled as a best-action query, with at most k queries available across T rounds.

With full feedback, the authors prove an optimal regret rate of Θ(min{√T, T/k}). The bound identifies when a limited query budget can improve the rate: the T/k term becomes favorable as k grows beyond the square-root scale. Thus, querying on only a sublinear number of rounds can still offer a substantial advantage.

The paper also considers a stricter setting where feedback is available only on queried rounds. Its tight rate is Θ(min{T/√k, T²/k²}), with the second term becoming advantageous beyond the T^(2/3) scale. This improves on the standard label-efficient prediction rate in the stated regime. The matching bounds quantify both the value and the limits of a budget for advance best-action information.
neurips-2024-online-learning-with-sublin.tldr: Tight regret bounds show when a sublinear budget of advance best-action queries improves online learning under two feedback models.

paragraphs: Sparse annotation allows an aerial detection dataset to cover more scenes without increasing the number of labeled objects. Training can then use pseudo-labels generated by the detector itself. However, fixed confidence thresholds are difficult to apply reliably when predicted aerial objects have imbalanced confidence scores.

Progressive Exploration-Conformal Learning treats pseudo-label selection as a learned decision process. Its explorer uses candidate characteristics and context between instances to decide which predictions to select. A separate evaluator assesses those choices using multiple clues and supplies feedback. The explorer learns an adaptive policy by maximizing cumulative reward from this selection process.

Selected pseudo-labels then guide further detector training, creating a progressive feedback loop between selection and detection. The approach therefore makes the selection policy part of the learning system instead of relying solely on a fixed cutoff. Evaluations on two public datasets report better performance than other state-of-the-art methods for sparsely annotated aerial object detection, supporting adaptive selection in the tested setting.
neurips-2024-progressive-exploration-con.tldr: PECL learns an adaptive pseudo-label selection policy to improve aerial object detection with sparse annotations.

paragraphs: Quasi-Bayesian prediction constructs a predictive distribution recursively, avoiding costly posterior sampling. Existing approaches work well for one-dimensional prediction, but their extensions to higher dimensions require restrictive dependence assumptions. This paper introduces QB-Vine to separate the problem of modeling each variable from modeling relationships among variables.

Using Sklar's theorem, the method combines one-dimensional predictive marginals with a multivariate copula. Recursive quasi-Bayesian updates handle the marginals, while expressive vine copulas represent dependence. Hyperparameters are tuned with robust divergences such as the energy score. The resulting density estimator is fully nonparametric and has an analytical form.

The authors establish a dimension-independent convergence rate in some situations, rather than as a universal property. Experiments show applicability to distributions of around 64 dimensions with around 200 training samples. They also report substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods with analytical forms on density estimation and supervised tasks. The contribution is a flexible route to high-dimensional prediction that retains an explicitly available density.
neurips-2024-quasi-bayes-meets-vines-6e1.tldr: QB-Vine combines recursive one-dimensional predictions with vine copulas to obtain flexible high-dimensional densities in analytical form.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter search usually compares candidate settings using the same training-validation split or cross-validation folds. This paper investigates changing those splits for every candidate instead. The central finding is that reshuffling often improves how the finally selected model performs on unseen data.

The theoretical analysis examines how reshuffling changes the limiting behavior of the validation loss surface. It also bounds expected regret in that regime, connecting the possible benefit to the signal and noise characteristics of the optimization problem. This makes the result conditional on the search problem's structure rather than a claim that reshuffling must always help.

A controlled simulation and a large realistic hyperparameter experiment support the analysis. The reported test performance is competitive with fixed splits overall, with particularly strong improvements for a single holdout protocol. Reshuffling can often make holdout competitive with standard cross-validation while costing less computation. The practical implication is that how data splits vary across configurations can materially affect the quality of hyperparameter selection.
neurips-2024-reshuffling-resampling-spli.tldr: Reshuffling data splits between hyperparameter configurations often improves generalization, especially for inexpensive single-holdout evaluation.

paragraphs: Active learning aims to spend labeling effort on examples that provide useful information. Many methods assume that a human will label every selected example. In consequential applications, however, people may reject requests because of domain knowledge, regulatory constraints, or reluctance to follow an algorithm's selection.

This paper formalizes that situation as Active Learning with Instance Rejection. Its SEL-BALD algorithms operate within deep Bayesian active learning and consider information acquisition for two models: the predictive machine learning model and a model of human discretion. This brings the behavior of the person deciding whether to label into the acquisition problem itself.

The approach matters because an informative example cannot provide its intended label information if the request is declined. Accounting for discretion addresses that mismatch between selection and actual feedback. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed algorithms' effectiveness. The contribution is an active learning formulation and corresponding methods that explicitly incorporate selective human participation when labeling is costly.
neurips-2024-sel-bald-deep-bayesian-acti.tldr: SEL-BALD incorporates human rejection of labeling requests into Bayesian active learning by learning about both predictions and human discretion.

paragraphs: Transferring cell-type annotations from scRNA-seq to unannotated scATAC-seq is difficult when the two data types differ and labeled cells are scarce. DANCE addresses this setting with a semi-supervised framework that expands available supervision while treating different target samples according to their relationship with the source data.

For scRNA-seq, optimal transport supplies pseudo-labels that are merged with existing labeled examples. For scATAC-seq, the method separates source-like samples from target-specific ones. Source-like samples receive consistency regularization under random perturbations. Target-specific samples receive candidate label sets, from which incorrect cell types are progressively removed to create additional supervision.

DANCE also generates virtual scRNA-seq examples through multi-sample Mixup guided by class-wise similarity, with the aim of reducing cell heterogeneity. These components jointly address scarce labels and differences across the two measurement types. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets suggest better performance than a range of state-of-the-art methods, supporting this differentiated approach to cross-omic transfer under cell-type scarcity.
neurips-2024-semi-supervised-knowledge-t.tldr: DANCE combines pseudo-labeling, sample-specific supervision, and Mixup to transfer cell types across omic data when labels are scarce.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, but repeated model evaluations make generation slow. Distillation aims to reduce that sampling cost, yet preparing a distilled model can itself require substantial fine-tuning. Simple and Fast Distillation addresses both the complexity of that preparation and the quality of few-step generation.

The method starts from a basic distillation approach and improves it by identifying several small but consequential factors affecting synthesis efficiency and quality. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and fine-tuning reductions of up to 1000 times. A single distilled model can also run with different numbers of function evaluations, allowing variation in sampling effort without requiring a separate model for each setting.

Experiments support a favorable balance between sample quality and fine-tuning cost. One reported example reaches an FID of 4.53 on CIFAR-10 with two function evaluations after 0.64 hours of fine-tuning on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. This illustrates the paper's emphasis on making accelerated generation economical to prepare as well as fast to run.
neurips-2024-simple-and-fast-distillatio.tldr: SFD simplifies diffusion distillation, sharply reduces reported fine-tuning costs, and supports multiple sampling budgets with one model.

paragraphs: Text embeddings represent text in a form that models can compare and use across tasks. English embeddings benefit from broad evaluation frameworks, but comparable coverage has been lacking for multilingual embeddings. The Scandinavian Embedding Benchmark addresses that gap by providing a dedicated framework for evaluating Scandinavian languages.

SEB covers 24 tasks, 10 subtasks, and four task categories. This breadth makes it possible to examine embedding performance across multiple kinds of use rather than relying on a handful of datasets. The authors use the framework to evaluate more than 26 models, including public and commercial offerings.

The evaluation reveals substantial performance differences between those offerings that were not previously captured by MTEB. The finding shows that expanding language-specific evaluation can expose distinctions left hidden by existing benchmark coverage. SEB is released openly and integrated with MTEB, making its Scandinavian tasks part of a wider evaluation ecosystem and providing a shared basis for assessing models in these languages.
neurips-2024-the-scandinavian-embedding-.tldr: SEB broadens Scandinavian text-embedding evaluation and reveals model performance disparities not previously captured by MTEB.

paragraphs: Finding a video moment becomes harder when several candidates partly match a query and only fine details distinguish the best one. This paper builds a benchmark around that challenge. It asks retrieval systems to identify precisely matching moments across a video collection rather than succeed through coarse understanding alone.

The VERIFIED annotation pipeline uses language and multimodal models to create detailed captions covering both static content and dynamics. Because generated captions can contain hallucinations, a dedicated noise evaluator filters inaccurate annotations. That evaluator is built by fine-tuning a video foundation model with challenging disturbed negatives and contrastive and matching losses.

The pipeline produces Charades-FIG, DiDeMo-FIG, and ActivityNet-FIG, which the authors report have high annotation quality. Evaluations of several state-of-the-art retrieval models reveal substantial room for improvement on these finer distinctions. The contribution combines a scalable annotation process with benchmarks designed to test whether systems understand the particular details needed to distinguish closely competing video moments.
neurips-2024-verified-a-video-corpus-mom.tldr: VERIFIED generates and filters detailed video captions to build benchmarks that expose gaps in fine-grained moment retrieval.

paragraphs: Video prediction can capture information about how an environment changes, which may help a robot choose actions. VidMan develops this idea through two-stage training. The motivation is to use limited robot trajectory data more effectively by explicitly connecting visual observations, learned dynamics, and action prediction.

First, the model learns to predict future visual trajectories from Open X-Embodiment data using video denoising diffusion. This stage develops awareness of environmental dynamics over an extended horizon. A layer-wise self-attention adapter then turns the model into an inverse dynamics model for predicting actions. Parameter sharing allows action prediction to draw on the dynamics knowledge learned during video training.

The authors report an 11.7% relative improvement over GR-1 on CALVIN and precision gains above 9% on a small-scale OXE dataset. These results support the value of learned visual dynamics for robot action prediction in the evaluated settings. The approach's central contribution is the transfer from predicting future observations to predicting actions through a shared model.
neurips-2024-vidman-exploiting-implicit-.tldr: VidMan transfers dynamics learned through video diffusion into robot action prediction, improving results on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Čech persistence diagrams summarize geometric and topological structure in data. They are often compared with Wasserstein distances, but understanding stability under those distances requires more than knowing that the diagrams are useful descriptors. This paper studies that issue when data are sampled from an m-dimensional submanifold of an ambient Euclidean space.

Under this manifold hypothesis, the authors establish that convergence in the Wasserstein metric OT_p occurs exactly when p exceeds m. The threshold therefore depends on the manifold's intrinsic dimension. This gives a precise condition for convergence in the studied setting, rather than a general stability assertion for every choice of metric exponent.

The paper also strengthens bottleneck stability results in this setting and proves laws of large numbers for total alpha-persistence, an aggregate summary of persistence. Finally, it connects these theoretical results to feature maps used in machine-learning applications of topological data analysis. Together, the findings clarify how sampling geometry influences both diagram comparison and representations built from diagrams.
neurips-2024-wasserstein-convergence-of-.tldr: For the studied manifold sampling setting, Čech persistence diagrams converge in Wasserstein OT_p exactly when p exceeds the manifold dimension.

paragraphs: A multimodal assistant may recognize a dog in an image without recognizing that it is a particular user's dog. This paper introduces personalization as a task for large multimodal models: learning a specific subject well enough to discuss it in conversation. The focus is on subject-specific understanding beyond generic category recognition.

Yo'LLaVA learns a representation of the subject from a handful of example images. It stores that representation in a set of latent tokens, giving the model a learned way to refer to and encode the subject. These tokens are intended to carry the visual information needed for personalized interactions.

Qualitative and quantitative analyses show that Yo'LLaVA learns the subject concept more efficiently with fewer tokens and captures visual attributes more effectively than strong prompting baselines, including LLaVA. The findings support learned subject representations as a route to personalization. They connect the representation's compactness with its ability to preserve the particular visual details that make a subject personally meaningful.
neurips-2024-yo-llava-your-personalized-.tldr: Yo'LLaVA learns compact subject-specific tokens from a few images to support personalized visual conversations.
